findings.paper_title: i7 Cabinet 120826 2026-27 Month 2 Financial Monitoring Report
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block cumulative deficit of £80m and growing, with out-of-authority placements surging and government relief contingent on reform plan
findings.detail: Doncaster faces an £80m cumulative DSG deficit by end of 2026/27 (forecast to reach £122.7m by 2027/28). Out-of-authority SEND placements are rising sharply: 217 at April 2026, 230 now, projected to 323 by March 2027. Government has committed to funding 90% via High Needs Stability Grant (90% of historic deficit, 90% of in-year deficits), but only if council produces 'satisfactory SEND reform plan.' The statutory override protecting councils from the deficit ends March 2028, when the council becomes liable for 10% (~£12.3m). If DfE funding drops to 75%, council liability rises to £23m.
findings.matters: This is a structural liability with a cliff edge. A £12-23m liability hitting the general fund in 2028 would require either massive reserves, cuts elsewhere, or borrowing. For lenders, it reveals latent liabilities and dependency on government relief that may not materialise. The reform plan condition adds execution risk.
findings.figures: £80m cumulative DSG deficit 2026/27; £122.7m projected 2027/28; out-of-authority placements 217→230→323 (projected); revised cumulative balance after 90% DfE funding £8m 2026/27, £12.3m council liability over 3 years; 75% funding scenario: £23m council liability; override ends 31 March 2028
findings.quote: cumulative overspend on DSG of £80.0m at 31 March 2027...The total placement numbers were 217 at 1st April 2026 and are currently 230, then projected to rise further to 323 by 31st March 2027...Should DfE funding reduce to, say, 75% in 2026/27 and 2027/28, the Council would need to find £23.0m in total

findings.paper_title: i7 Cabinet 120826 2026-27 Month 2 Financial Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand outrunning budget by £2.5m-£3.56m, driven by higher residential care placements and homecare unit costs
findings.detail: Residential care overspends £1.93m due to 718 older people (vs 701 budgeted, costing £0.79m) and 625 extra short-stay days per month. findings.matters: Adult care is both structural (demographic) and volatile. A £2.5m+ overspend in Month 2 of a service that serves vulnerable people signals either policy/demographic shift or budget planning failure. Both matter to lenders: unplanned spending risks reserves, and if driven by demographics, it signals recurring pressure.
findings.figures: Older people residential: 718 clients vs 701 budgeted (£0.79m overspend); homecare unit cost £1,765 vs £1,571 budgeted; short-stay additional days ~625/month (£0.47m overspend); total Adults directorate overspend £3.56m

findings.paper_title: i7 Cabinet 120826 2026-27 Month 2 Financial Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Service budget overspend of £6.2m at Month 2 requiring full contingency depletion
findings.detail: The council is 6.2% over budget (£6.2m on £81.3m service budgets) by the end of Month 2 — only two months into the financial year. Using the full £5.57m contingency leaves only £0.6m headroom. The council explicitly warns this 'places the Council in a challenging financial position at a very early stage of the financial year and significantly reduces flexibility to respond to further pressures that may emerge.'
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial resilience by cash position, budget control, and room to absorb shocks. Depleting contingency by Month 2 signals either structural spending problems or that the budget was built with insufficient contingency for real demand.
findings.figures: £6.2m overspend against £81.3m service budget; £5.57m contingency fully applied, leaving £0.6m buffer before risk reserve
findings.quote: requiring the full contingency budget to be utilised by Month 2 places the Council in a challenging financial position at a very early stage of the financial year and significantly reduces flexibility to respond to further pressures that may emerge

findings.matters: A major capital project with borrowing commitment is proceeding despite internal audit noting it lacks sufficient officer capacity and governance maturity. findings.paper_title: i12 Strategic Risk Deep Dive DSG SEND Reform_TT final_v2
findings.headline: 2026/27 DSG forecast shows cumulative overspend of £79m, driven by continued demand growth and insufficient local specialist capacity
findings.detail: The forecast for 2026/27 projects a cumulative DSG overspend of £79m. The primary drivers are rising demand for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) and insufficient local specialist provision, forcing reliance on expensive out-of-area and independent placements. Specialist place shortfall is projected to rise from 388 in 2025/26 to 661 in 2026/27 to 924 in 2027/28 without mitigation.
findings.matters: This shows structural financial pressure in a major service area. Demand is outpacing the council's capacity to provide services, driving rising costs.
findings.figures: £79m cumulative overspend projected for 2026/27; specialist place shortfall rising from 388 (2025/26) to 661 (2026/27) to 924 (2027/28)
findings.quote: The 2026/27 forecast based on current assumptions is a cumulative DSG overspend of £79m at 31st March 2027. A key driver of this risk is that demand for specialist provision is growing faster than local capacity. Our SEND Sufficiency Business Case identifies a projected specialist place shortfall rising from 388 in 2025/26 to 661 in 2026/27 and 924 in 2027/28 if no mitigating action is taken.

findings.paper_title: i12 Strategic Risk Deep Dive DSG SEND Reform_TT final_v2
findings.headline: Significant uncertainty on in-year DSG deficit funding for 2026/27 and 2027/28; if funding drops to 75%, council faces additional £20.3m pressure
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget assumes 90% government funding will continue for in-year DSG deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28. However, the government has only committed to an 'appropriate and proportionate approach' without detail. A scenario modelled with 75% funding would create an additional £20.3m pressure, of which £10m is reflected in the MTFS and £10.3m is residual unbudgeted risk.
findings.matters: This represents material unquantified exposure to budget risk. The council's financial planning depends on assumptions about government funding that have not been formally confirmed.
findings.figures: 75% funding scenario creates £20.3m additional pressure; £10m already in MTFS; £10.3m residual risk exposure unbudgeted
findings.quote: The Council's 2026/27 budget assumes that the 90% funding level will continue to apply to in-year DSG deficits in both 2026/27 and 2027/28. However, this remains subject to uncertainty pending confirmation of the Government's detailed approach. As part of the assessment of the adequacy of reserves, a scenario has also been modelled whereby the proportionate funding reduces to 75%. Under this scenario, the Council would face a total additional financial pressure of £20.3m. Of this amount, £10m has already been reflected within the Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS), leaving a residual risk exposure of £10.3m.

findings.paper_title: i12 Strategic Risk Deep Dive DSG SEND Reform_TT final_v2
findings.headline: Statutory override ends 31st March 2028, creating a hard deadline for deficit resolution
findings.detail: The statutory override that currently allows councils to carry forward DSG deficits expires at the end of March 2028. By that point, the council must have resolved or funded its residual DSG deficit. Even with 90% government support for historic deficits, the council will retain a material residual DSG pressure once the override ends.
findings.matters: This is a hard constraint on the council's financial position. The council cannot carry deficits indefinitely and faces pressure to balance its DSG position before the deadline.
findings.figures: 31st March 2028 deadline; projected residual DSG pressure after 90% government support
findings.quote: The statutory override in place to enable the DSG deficit to be carried forward ends 31st March 2028, but the High Needs Stability Grant funding will help to reduce the deficit it as outlined in this report.

findings.paper_title: i12 Strategic Risk Deep Dive DSG SEND Reform_TT final_v2
findings.headline: DSG deficit of £50.9m by March 2026 with 90% government funding dependent on plan approval
findings.detail: The council has accumulated a cumulative DSG deficit of £50.9m by 31st March 2026, with 2025/26 showing an in-year overspend of £13.3m. The government has indicated it will fund 90% of the historic deficit (£45.8m) if the council's Local SEND Reform Plan is approved. However, this funding is not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale of the deficit, how it is being funded, and the conditionality attached to that funding.
findings.figures: £50.9m cumulative deficit at 31st March 2026; potential £45.8m of 90% government funding; 2025/26 in-year overspend of £13.3m
findings.quote: the consultation has now closed, and the Government's formal response is still awaited. While the final national reform framework is not yet fully settled, local activity is already live. Local authorities have been required to develop and submit Local SEND Reform Plans, and approval of those plans is the condition for access to the High Needs Stability Grant, which is intended to cover up to 90% of eligible historic DSG deficits recognised at 31st March 2026.

findings.paper_title: SYAC Motion to Rescind Borrowing decision Council report
findings.headline: Subsidy control referral to CMA Subsidy Advice Unit raised compliance concerns requiring ongoing assessment updates.
findings.detail: The scale of public subsidy (loan from council to FlyDoncaster Ltd) triggered a mandatory referral to the CMA's Subsidy Advice Unit in November 2024. The SAU report (January 2025) is non-binding but flagged six areas for improvement. The council must update its subsidy assessment to reflect current information and address SAU recommendations. If any subsidy challenge is made during the challenge period, further funding commitments may be restricted, potentially disrupting delivery timescales.
findings.matters: Subsidy control challenges can delay or halt funding. A lender needs to understand that regulatory risk remains around the entire funding structure and that compliance requirements could impose unexpected costs or delays.
findings.figures: Subsidy referral submitted 29 November 2024; SAU report 22 January 2025; six areas for improvement identified; 30-day challenge period after subsidy approval
findings.quote: the level of subsidy proposed from CDC to FlyDoncaster Ltd, in the form of the loan, triggered the requirement to make a referral to the Subsidy Advice Unit (SAU) at the CMA to obtain feedback on CDC's analysis of the subsidy against the principles in Subsidy Control Act 2022.

findings.paper_title: SYAC Motion to Rescind Borrowing decision Council report
findings.headline: Programme requires SYMCA grant agreement with detailed controls including step-in rights, board representation, and subsidy compliance conditions.
findings.detail: SYMCA has approved up to £159.52m in gainshare funding for reopening and operation of the airport. The grant is conditional on a series of precedent conditions and contractual controls: SYMCA board representation, right to take assignment of lease (step-in), restrictions on lease variation without approval, controls on company indebtedness, and proof of subsidy compliance. SYMCA approval is explicitly for airport reopening only; if the airport doesn't reopen, the funding mechanism would not apply to closure costs.
findings.matters: SYMCA controls the funding and can override council decisions through its contractual rights. This reduces council autonomy and creates external dependency risk. The council cannot resolve the closure-cost funding gap by accessing the gainshare.
findings.figures: £159.52m SYMCA gainshare approval for reopening and operation; conditions include SYMCA board rights, step-in on lease, subsidy control conditions
findings.quote: SYMCA's approval of the use of gainshare funding was explicitly provided to facilitate the reopening and future operation of Doncaster Sheffield Airport. The SYMCA Board report considered in September 2025 stated that, "subject to the entering into of a Funding Agreement, funding is approved to enable the re‑opening and operation of DSA at a total level of up to £159.52m." On this basis, if the reopening of the airport is not achieved, the existing approval would not provide a mechanism for gainshare funding to be applied toward closure costs.

findings.paper_title: SYAC Motion to Rescind Borrowing decision Council report
findings.headline: Superior lease includes break clauses and termination options that could force council exit before commitment period ends.
findings.detail: The council committed to a 125-year lease starting 20 March 2024. The lease includes mutual break clauses at 7 years (2031) if the airport has not been operational or has ceased for 12 consecutive months. Additionally, the landlord can terminate if planning permission is not received within specific timeframes. Amended lease terms have been negotiated to move break points from 2031 to 2036 onwards with higher passenger thresholds, but these remain material risks.
findings.matters: Lease termination clauses create exit risk if the airport fails to open or operate within agreed parameters. A lender needs to understand that the council's long-term lease commitment is conditional and could be triggered involuntarily.
findings.figures: 125-year lease term; 7-year break clause at 2031 on original terms; revised terms push options to 2036 with 10-year or 5-year intervals; passenger thresholds range 1,000,000 (2036) to 2,300,000 (2056)
findings.quote: The lease is for 125 years covering the former Airport site (DSAL) & DSA04 which is an airside development site. Includes a mutual break clause at 7 years, based on 2 years to become operational and further 5 years, covering if the whole or substantially the whole of the premises has not been used as an Operational Civil Airport.

findings.paper_title: SYAC Motion to Rescind Borrowing decision Council report
findings.headline: Easter 2028 opening date is critical to financial viability; a 12-month delay makes the programme financially unviable within the funding envelope.
findings.detail: The airport must begin passenger operations by Easter 2028 to meet financial projections. Any delay to the following winter or summer season cascades into significant financial pressure. A 12-month delay would reduce projected income by £36.1m over the main loan period to 2034/35, while only £24.3m of expenditure can be deferred, creating a net adverse impact of £11.8m and rendering the programme unaffordable.
findings.matters: This shows the thinness of the financial model. The programme depends entirely on meeting a specific operational date. Lenders must understand that construction delays, regulatory approvals, or staffing shortages could breach the funding envelope.
findings.figures: Easter 2028 target opening date; 12-month delay = £36.1m income loss; £24.3m expenditure deferrals possible; £11.8m net adverse impact
findings.quote: a 12-month delay would reduce projected income by £36.1m over the main loan period to 2034/35. While this delay would also reduce some forecast expenditure and allow certain costs to be deferred (for example, additional staffing), many costs are fixed and would remain committed... resulting in a net adverse financial impact of £11.8m, up to 2034/35.

findings.paper_title: SYAC Motion to Rescind Borrowing decision Council report
findings.headline: Failure to fund closure costs if the programme stops would trigger a potential Section 114 notice from the S151 Officer.
findings.detail: The report explicitly warns that if the council cannot identify funding to meet the £48.6m closure liability, the Section 151 Officer would be required to consider whether to issue a Section 114 notice under the Local Government Finance Act 1988, which signals statutory inability to balance the budget.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a serious warning that a council is approaching insolvency. It affects creditworthiness, borrowing costs, and stakeholder confidence. Lenders view councils that trigger these notices as higher risk.
findings.figures: £48.6m liability; Section 114 notice is statutory obligation if funding gap not closed
findings.quote: Failure to do so would increase the risk of the Section 151 Officer needing to consider statutory duties under Section 114 of the Local Government Finance Act 1988.

findings.paper_title: SYAC Motion to Rescind Borrowing decision Council report
findings.headline: If the motion passes and borrowing is rescinded, the council faces quantified unfunded liabilities of approximately £48.6m to 2031 for lease, site costs, and redundancy.
findings.detail: Rescinding the borrowing decision would halt the programme. The council would remain liable for lease payments, site management costs, and redundancy costs estimated at £48.6m through 2031. This figure excludes further uncertainties around full redundancy costs and contract cessation. Alternative funding would need to be identified immediately or the council faces a Section 114 notice scenario.
findings.matters: A sudden £48.6m liability without a funding source is a major financial shock for a council's balance sheet. It signals weak programme governance if the council enters long-term lease commitments without a clear exit or completion strategy.
findings.figures: £48.6m quantified future liabilities to 2031; £20.7m already spent 2023/24-2025/26
findings.quote: Current estimates indicate quantified future liabilities of approximately £48.6m to 2031, with further uncertainty around redundancy and contract cessation costs.

findings.paper_title: SYAC Motion to Rescind Borrowing decision Council report
findings.headline: Borrowing of up to £57m approved in November 2025 to bridge timing gap between airport programme spending and SYMCA gainshare grant receipt.
findings.detail: The borrowing is not additional long-term funding but a cashflow mechanism intended to be repaid over time using SYMCA gainshare grant. Peak borrowing estimated at £57m in year 2032/33, declining thereafter. The council argues borrowing costs will be funded entirely by the £193m total funding envelope and does not impact wider council budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the borrowing structure, repayment source, and whether the council's financial plan is credible. This is the largest active borrowing commitment.
findings.figures: £57m peak borrowing; £193m total funding envelope; £113.6m cumulative funding vs £153.6m cumulative costs by 2034/35
findings.quote: The borrowing decision approved in November 2025 allows the Council to manage the timing difference between programme expenditure and the receipt of anticipated SYMCA gainshare funding. The programme requires borrowing of up to £57m at peak cashflow.

findings.paper_title: 2026_27 TMSS Council
findings.headline: HRA borrowing costs are higher than General Fund and rising relative to HRA revenue
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account debt carries a 5.09% average rate vs 4.79% for General Fund. The HRA debt-to-revenue ratio for 2026/27 is 36.39% and debt per dwelling is rising to £13,616. HRA borrowing is forecast at £269.304m in 2026/27, growing to £345.304m by 2029/30, with higher interest rates locked in.
findings.matters: Higher borrowing costs in the HRA mean less money for repairs and maintenance. Rising debt-per-dwelling signals financial strain in the housing revenue model.
findings.figures: HRA average interest rate 5.09% (2024/25) forecast to fall to 4.4% (2029/30); HRA debt £239.304m (2025/26) rising to £345.304m (2029/30); debt per dwelling £13,616 (2026/27) rising to £17,170 (2029/30)
findings.quote: The average interest rate on the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) debt is higher than the General Fund (GF) debt as that pool contains a higher proportion of older debt taken out at higher interest rates.

findings.paper_title: 2026_27 TMSS Council
findings.headline: Very high net financing need of £87.962m in 2026/27 alone, plus £57m airport borrowing starting 2027/28
findings.detail: The council must borrow nearly £88m in 2026/27 just to fund its capital programme. On top of this, £57m in airport reopening borrowing is planned for 2027/28 (already approved November 2025). Total capital spend of £248m in 2026/27 is among the highest in the local authority sector, heavily dependent on borrowing and reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: High capital demand combined with depleting reserves and forced borrowing creates a financing squeeze. The council's debt trajectory is steep: CFR rising from £771.5m (2025/26) to £962m (2029/30).
findings.figures: 2026/27 net financing need £87.962m; 2026/27 total capital expenditure £248.195m; airport borrowing £57m; CFR growth of £78.954m in 2026/27 alone

findings.paper_title: 2026_27 TMSS Council
findings.headline: Council betting that interest rates will fall; if they don't, short-term borrowing costs spike
findings.detail: The strategy relies entirely on short-term borrowing until rates fall to the assumed 3.5% neutral level. Currently 35% of debt is 30–50 year fixed; new borrowing is only short-term. If rates stay elevated or fall slower than forecast, the council faces refinancing risk on maturing short-term debt at potentially higher rates, and the interest bill grows materially.
findings.matters: A miscast interest rate forecast directly hits the revenue budget. The council's £5.698m borrowing cost forecast assumes rate falls that may not materialise.
findings.figures: Forecast CFR 2026/27 £850.459m; current external debt £574m; average GF interest rate forecast to fall from 4.72% (2025/26) to 3.8% (2029/30); HRA rate from 5.01% to 4.4%
findings.quote: only borrowing in the short term for cash flow purposes whilst borrowing rates are at current levels. Despite the Bank of England base rate decreases that have taken place in 2025/26 the borrowing rates are still high due to other economic factors

findings.paper_title: 2026_27 TMSS Council
findings.headline: Under-borrowed position cannot be sustained as reserves deplete and DSG deficit grows
findings.detail: The council admits explicitly that its £64m under-borrowed position is unsustainable long-term. Reserves are falling sharply—from £89m (2025/26) to £4.8m (2026/27) to negative territory from 2027/28 onwards due to the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit. The council will eventually be forced to borrow at whatever rates prevail rather than by choice.
findings.matters: A forced borrower has no negotiating power. Once reserves are exhausted, the council must borrow regardless of interest rates. This creates refinancing risk and uncertain future debt costs.
findings.figures: Core funds falling from £89.293m (2025/26) to -£5.126m (2028/29); DSG deficit of £51.1m with only 90% funded by government
findings.quote: The current extent of the under borrowing cannot be sustained in the long term. The reserves and balances are starting to be required as well as the actual amount of reserves available for use being reduced by the increasing dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27 - 2028-29_Redacted
findings.headline: Chief Financial Officer signals that the main challenge for 2026/27 is 'managers to continue to mitigate and manage the pressures to deliver spend within the approved budget'.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer (CFO) explicitly states the 'main challenge' is not budget planning but in-year delivery. Despite identifying additional savings, the underlying pressure is so significant that active mitigation throughout the year is required just to stay within budget.
findings.matters: When the chief finance officer flags delivery (not planning) as the main challenge, it signals execution risk and tight margins. The budget is balanced on assumptions requiring constant management throughout the year.
findings.figures: No specific figures; statement of delivery risk
findings.quote: Although some additional savings have been identified through the process, the main challenge for 2026/27 will be, for managers to continue to mitigate and manage the pressures to deliver spend within the approved budget.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27 - 2028-29_Redacted
findings.headline: 43% of planned Core Spending Power growth depends on Council Tax increases; economic outlook is weak growth and rising unemployment.
findings.detail: The settlement assumes 5% per annum Council Tax increases, and 43% of total CSP growth is projected to come from discretionary tax rises. The council's economic outlook notes 'weak growth and increasing unemployment', which threatens Council Tax collection rates and the council's ability to levy increases at assumed levels.
findings.matters: A budget heavily dependent on discretionary tax rises is vulnerable to collection shortfalls or political resistance. Weak economic outlook reduces the likelihood of achieving assumed growth.
findings.figures: 43% of CSP increase from Council Tax; 5% per annum assumed; weak growth and rising unemployment in outlook
findings.quote: The share of new funding that is coming from assumed increases in Council Tax (5%pa) is very high over the 3 years – 43% of the total CSP increase is due to Council Tax increases. The wider economic outlook (weak growth and increasing unemployment) also creates uncertainty around the Council's other main sources of income (Business Rates and Council Tax).

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27 - 2028-29_Redacted
findings.headline: Uncommitted reserves of £12.7m represent only 7 days' spending for a £720m annual budget; external auditors have flagged the need to build reserves.
findings.detail: Uncommitted reserves stand at £12.7m, against identified risks of £12.0m, leaving only £0.7m for truly unplanned spending. For a council spending ~£720m per year, this provides 7 days of contingency. External auditors flagged low reserves in their 2024/25 Annual Auditor letter. The council is committed to increasing reserves, but this has not yet happened.
findings.matters: Thin reserves limit the council's capacity to absorb unexpected shocks (pay awards, demand spikes, income shortfalls). For a lender, this indicates financial vulnerability and limited buffer.
findings.figures: £12.7m uncommitted; £12.0m identified risks; £720m annual spend; 7 days contingency; £0.7m unallocated buffer
findings.quote: Appendix H provides the risk assessment of the Council's level of reserves.  It shows risks with estimated value of £12.0m (this is £0.7m below the expected balance level of uncommitted reserves available of £12.7m, leaving a balance for any unforeseen spend).  This level of uncommitted reserves is not excessive for a Council of our size, which spends circa. £720m a year; £12.7m would only run the Council for 7 days.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27 - 2028-29_Redacted
findings.headline: Significant asset maintenance backlog unfunded: ageing estate, parks, highways and infrastructure described as 'in desperate need of investment'.
findings.detail: Due to financial constraints, the council has not provided revenue funding for capital costs to maintain its estate. Only essential health-and-safety schemes are funded, leaving 'several risks that haven't been funded'. The council acknowledges these matters 'have been previously deferred subject to funding becoming available, however are becoming more urgent'.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance creates hidden liabilities that eventually force spending, often in emergencies. For a lender, this represents a contingent liability and future spending pressure.
findings.figures: No quantification in paper; described as 'desperate need'
findings.quote: due to the financial challenges, it has not been possible to provide the required revenue funding for the increasing capital costs required to maintain our ageing estate across the borough.  The resources continue to be prioritised to essential schemes based on health and safety assessments; as a result, there are several risks that haven't been funded and our ageing estate, wide geography (parks, public right of way, trees, highways infrastructure) are in desperate need of investment.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27 - 2028-29_Redacted
findings.headline: Previous year's approved savings targets are being written off because they are now 'no longer thought to be achievable'.
findings.detail: In February 2025, £2.3m of savings were approved (£1.7m in 2026/27, £0.6m in 2027/28). In this budget, £0.2m of these targets has been removed because they are 'no longer thought to be achievable'. This indicates prior savings plans failed to deliver.
findings.matters: A pattern of savings being revised downward signals delivery credibility issues. A lender needs confidence that the £3.7m in new savings proposed will land, but track record is mixed.
findings.figures: £0.2m reduction in previously approved targets; £2.3m approved Feb 2025
findings.quote: A reduction of £0.2m has been included in the new savings referred to below, to recognise previously approved targets, no longer thought to be achievable.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27 - 2028-29_Redacted
findings.headline: Children's social care savings plan significantly behind schedule: out-of-authority placements reducing much slower than planned, creating £3.7m 2026/27 pressure.
findings.detail: The council planned to reduce out-of-authority placements from 54 in April 2023 to 36.5 in 2026/27, but 'reductions haven't happened as quickly as expected'. This creates a £3.7m pressure in 2026/27, reducing only to £1.5m by 2028/29. A major savings plan is tracking significantly behind target.
findings.matters: A lender assesses credibility on whether savings plans deliver. A £3.7m miss in one key area signals execution risk and questions whether the council's £3.7m of 2026/27 savings targets will be achieved.
findings.figures: 54 placements April 2023; target 36.5 in 2026/27; £3.7m pressure 2026/27, reducing to £1.5m by 2028/29
findings.quote: Progress has been made in reducing the numbers of out of authority placements from 54 in April 2023 to a planned average of 36.5 in 2026/27, 31 in 2027/28 and 28 in 2028/29.  The reductions haven't happened as quickly as expected which is why there is a £3.7m pressure in 2026/27, reducing to £1.5m in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27 - 2028-29_Redacted
findings.headline: Adult Social Care pressures more than double over the MTFS period: £12.3m rising to £22.9m by 2028/29, including £3m unfunded National Living Wage costs.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is the single largest service pressure (residential care, supported living, homecare). Fee rate inflation alone rises from £5.0m to £13.9m. The National Living Wage increase totals £3.0m and does not attract additional government funding, forcing the council to absorb this from its own resources.
findings.matters: Social care is the most volatile pressure on councils. A lender must assess whether the council can absorb costs nearly doubling and whether demand-reduction strategies (Radical Efficiency programme) will deliver tangible results.
findings.figures: £12.3m in 2026/27 increasing to £22.9m by 2028/29; fee inflation £5.0m→£13.9m; National Living Wage £3.0m unfunded
findings.quote: Adult Social Care service pressures and contract inflationary increases amount to £12.3m in 2026/27 and increasing to £22.9m by 2028/29.  This includes £5.0m for fee rate inflation in 2026/27, increasing to £13.9m by 2028/29, including the impact of the Government National Living Wage increase (which totals £3.0m and does not attract additional government funding).

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27 - 2028-29_Redacted
findings.headline: Over £13m of ongoing base budget depends on Recovery Grant guaranteed only through 2028/29, creating a potential funding cliff from 2029/30.
findings.detail: The council is using temporary Recovery Grant funding (£12.5m–£13.9m per year) to meet ongoing base budget needs. If this grant is not available after 2028/29, the council faces a 'substantial funding shortfall and savings to be identified'. The grant sits outside the government's calculation of relative need and may not be renewed.
findings.matters: A lender must identify structural funding vulnerabilities. Funding ongoing base budget with temporary grants creates a cliff-edge liability that could force emergency borrowing or deep service cuts.
findings.figures: £12.5m in 2026/27, increasing to £13.9m by 2028/29; if unavailable in 2029/30, creates substantial shortfall
findings.quote: Recovery Grant (£12.5m in 2026/27, increasing to £13.9m by 2028/29) is only guaranteed for the multi-year period.  This presents a financial risk, in that ongoing base budget is being funded using this grant, which if it is not available in 2029/30 would mean a substantial funding shortfall and savings to be identified.

findings.paper_title: HRA Council Report 26.02.26
findings.headline: Awaab's Law damp and mould compliance mandates create new cost pressure with strict regulatory deadlines
findings.detail: The Awaab's Law mandate (in force 27 October 2025) requires social landlords to address damp and mould within strict timeframes. This has created a £271k cost pressure for additional staffing, products and specialist IT software. Beyond this, the council budgeted a further £1.0m for broader damp/mould demand, which tenants identified as their top service priority.
findings.matters: New regulatory mandate with fixed compliance deadlines creates cost and reputational risk; failure to comply could trigger enforcement action
findings.figures: £271k for Awaab's Law compliance (staffing, products, software); £1.0m total damp/mould budget allocation
findings.quote: Awaab's Law, which came into force on 27 October 2025, mandates social landlords to address issues of damp and mould in their properties within strict timeframes. In response to this additional staffing, mould washing products and specialist IT software is required to address these issues which has resulted in a cost pressure within the HRA of £271k

findings.paper_title: HRA Council Report 26.02.26
findings.headline: St Leger Homes management fee increases £3.1m (6.8%) on pay awards, outpacing 4.8% rent growth
findings.detail: The council's contractor, St Leger Homes of Doncaster (SLHD), management fee rises from approximately £42.7m to £45.8m, a £3.1m increase driven by pay awards and inflation. Since SLHD provides the majority of HRA services, this cost inflation outpacing rent income growth creates structural budget pressure.
findings.matters: If service costs inflate faster than the 4.8% maximum allowed rent increase each year, the gap will widen, forcing either service cuts or rent policy changes
findings.figures: £3.1m increase to SLHD management fee (6.8% growth); £45.8m total fee; rent increase 4.8%
findings.quote: The majority of HRA services are provided by St. Leger Homes of Doncaster (SLHD). The management fee paid to SLHD is increased by a net £3.1m to reflect increases in salaries (pay award), inflationary increases and other changes. The management fee paid from the HRA for 2026/27 is £45.8m

findings.paper_title: HRA Council Report 26.02.26
findings.headline: Right to Buy acceleration reduces housing stock and ongoing rental income
findings.detail: Following the October 2024 government announcement reducing RTB discounts, the council received 359 RTB applications between October and 20 November 2024. Sales have continued elevated: 58 completed by 31 December 2025, averaging 1.49 per week versus 1.23 per week in the prior year. This trend reduces the asset base and future rental income.
findings.matters: Stock loss directly reduces the revenue base; projections must account for this elevated RTB rate continuing if policy remains unchanged
findings.figures: 359 RTB applications Oct-Nov 2024; 58 completed sales by 31 Dec 2025; 1.49 sales/week vs 1.23 prior year
findings.quote: Following announcements in the Government's October 2024 budget to significantly reduce the maximum discounts available for tenants wishing to purchase their home under the right to buy (RTB) scheme after 20 November 2024, we had a significant increase in RTB applications (359 applications received between the October budget and 20 November 2024 deadline)... The number of RTB sales continues to be monitored and total sales to the 31st December 2025 were 58 giving an average of 1.49 sales per week (compared to 1.23 per week as of December 2024)

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Children's Social Care placement costs rising due to increased complexity and out-of-authority placements averaging 36.5; costs growing faster than budget
findings.detail: Children's social care is experiencing 'increased complexity resulting in higher costs' and an average of 36.5 out-of-authority placements. The paper budgets for this but also notes mitigation strategy (increasing in-house capacity) will take time to deliver.
findings.matters: Rising children's social care costs are a sector-wide pressure; councils with above-average complexity face sustained cost growth that will persist across the MTFS.
findings.figures: 36.5 average out-of-authority placements; 24% increase in short breaks provision (292 children); £0.7m budget pressure for short breaks

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Ageing estate maintenance backlog unfunded; capital investment insufficient to meet essential infrastructure repair needs
findings.detail: Despite additional capital funding, the council cannot fund required maintenance of its estate. Only essential health-and-safety schemes are being prioritised; 'several risks that haven't been funded' remain, including parks, public rights of way, trees, and highways infrastructure.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance on core infrastructure creates deteriorating asset base and future cost escalation; lenders assess council asset condition as a credit indicator.
findings.figures: None specific; nature of backlog qualitative
findings.quote: Although additional funding has been incorporated for capital investment in our assets, particularly our buildings and roads, it is still not possible to provide the required revenue funding for all the increasing capital costs required to maintain our ageing estate across the borough.

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Asset rationalisation programme already underdelivered by £0.569m against target with no published recovery plan
findings.detail: The asset disposal programme has missed targets and budgets have been 'rebased' rather than recovered. No recovery plan is published, suggesting targets are being softened rather than missed targets being recovered.
findings.matters: Underperforming asset sales indicate difficulty realizing expected capital proceeds; if asset income disappoints, capital and revenue programmes may need to be cut.
findings.figures: Underdelivery: £0.569m
findings.quote: Asset rationalisation that has already underdelivered by £0.569m against its original target, with no published recovery plan in the 2026/27 papers.

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Commercial property income declining due to weak city centre demand; rents described as 'increasingly difficult to let'
findings.detail: Commercial property income is failing to meet targets because 'commercial property is increasingly difficult to let due to the reduced demand for city centre locations.' This is presented as a structural market pressure rather than temporary shortfall.
findings.matters: Weakening property income reflects sector-wide decline in city centre occupancy; lenders should expect this revenue pressure to persist.
findings.figures: None specified; described qualitatively
findings.quote: commercial property is increasingly difficult to let due to the reduced demand for city centre locations; these service changes and financial pressures have been previously communicated and detailed in the quarterly Finance and Performance Improvement reports.

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Culture and Commercialisation service £1m over budget in 2025/26 with ongoing pressures; Reform UK increases income target by further £200k
findings.detail: Culture is running £1m over budget in 2025/26 and 'pressures are ongoing.' The Reform UK amendment adds a new £200k income target on top of existing £0.96m savings target. The finance director notes it is 'unrealistic to assume that the full £1m can be delivered in 2026/27' and prior Section 25 statements have flagged concerns about income generation in this sector during the cost-of-living crisis.
findings.matters: An underperforming service with escalating income targets is vulnerable to shortfall; the auditor has already identified this sector as a concern.
findings.figures: 2025/26 forecast overspend: £1m. Reform UK additional target: £200k. Existing Culture savings target: £0.96m
findings.quote: The Mayor's budget proposals retain the assumption that the overall previous saving target should be delivered, and pressures managed across the 3-year period... This proposal increases the current income savings targets by a further £200k.

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Trade waste service forecast overbudget by £0.66m in 2025/26; income targets consistently missed for multiple years despite service generating surplus
findings.detail: The service is currently £0.66m over budget due to loss of major customers in a competitive market. The paper states 'it has not been possible to achieve the budgeted income target' despite additional investment. While the service generates net surplus (£0.6m in 2024/25), it persistently misses profit targets.
findings.matters: A revenue stream that consistently underperforms signals weak pricing power or declining service demand; repeated target revisions suggest budgets remain optimistic.
findings.figures: 2025/26 forecast overspend: £0.66m. 2024/25: income £2.0m, expenditure £1.4m, net surplus £0.6m
findings.quote: Trade Waste is expected to be over budget by £0.66m due to unrealisable income targets in a challenging economic climate and competitive commercial market.

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Contingency fund reduced from £6m to £5m at same time financial risks increase, reducing in-year flexibility for pressures
findings.detail: The Reform UK amendment cuts contingency by £1m precisely when social care pressures are described as 'difficult to predict' and a specific £3.4m risk is identified in Children's Continuing Health Care contributions.
findings.matters: Contingency is the buffer for unexpected in-year costs; reducing it while risks rise signals tighter margin and weaker resilience.
findings.figures: Contingency £6m → £5m (£1m reduction); CHC Children risk: £3.4m
findings.quote: The Reform UK budget amendment reduces the contingency to £5m, whilst at the same time increasing the financial risk.

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: External auditor flagged that without reserve strategy development, a Section 114 notice may become necessary within this MTFS period
findings.detail: Grant Thornton made a key recommendation to develop a reserve strategy. The finance director states 'without this mechanism for protecting against overspends a Section 114 report may become necessary' and notes 'given the underlying service pressures and increased savings requirements this may be required within this MTFS period' (2026–2029).
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal governance failure and default signal; the auditor's explicit warning indicates the council is at material risk of losing financial control.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: The External Auditor has made a recommendation for the Council to develop a reserve strategy because without this mechanism for protecting against overspends a Section 114 report may become necessary.

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Reform UK amendment requires £2.1m additional savings from areas already heavily targeted in prior budgets, raising delivery risk
findings.detail: The amendment increases required savings to £2.1m in 2026/27 from agency, income generation, management cuts, and contingency. The finance director states 'The savings are mostly from areas that have been targeted previously, and either delivered reducing the capacity to deliver further savings or extremely challenging to delivered for various reasons.'
findings.matters: Savings from already-squeezed areas are harder to achieve; if they slip, the council will need emergency measures or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £2.1m additional savings 2026/27; £0.4m in 2027/28; £0.4m in 2028/29; further £1.359m to be identified for 2027/28
findings.quote: The Reform UK budget amendment increases the risks associated with the delivery of savings, increasing the ongoing savings to be delivered by £2.100m in 2026/27, £0.400m in 2027/28 and a further £0.400m in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Funding cliff-edge in 2029/30 when Recovery Grant ends; potential shortfall of £9.9m rising to £15m if Reform UK savings not delivered
findings.detail: The settlement includes a Recovery Grant only guaranteed through 2028/29. The finance director identifies this as 'a financial risk' and notes that if savings targets are not met, the hole widens from £9.9m to £15m. This cliff will need review in 2027/28 budget setting.
findings.matters: A structural funding cliff arriving in just 3 years creates severe refinancing and service sustainability risk; lenders need to see a recovery plan now.
findings.figures: £9.9m shortfall in 2029/30 (base case); £15m if Reform UK savings not delivered; Recovery Grant £2.6m in 2026/27, £10m total over 3 years
findings.quote: The settlement also hasn't been as positive as originally anticipated based on the summer consultation. This presents a financial risk in that ongoing base budget is being funded using this grant, which if it is not available in 2029/30 would mean a substantial funding shortfall of £9.9m and further savings to be identified.

findings.paper_title: Updated Section 25 including Reform UK Budget Amendment (final)
findings.headline: Reform UK budget amendment reduces immediate funding by £4.584m and cumulatively by £14.6m over three years
findings.detail: The amendment caps council tax increases at 2% instead of the planned 4.99%, materially reducing the council's revenue base. The finance director explicitly states this 'reduces the ongoing revenue income available to the Council to fund services and therefore further exacerbates the future financial sustainability risk.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council has materially less recurring revenue than previously assumed to service debt and fund core services.
findings.figures: £4.584m reduction 2026/27; £0.275m reduction 2027/28; £0.292m reduction 2028/29; £14.6m cumulative over 3 years
findings.quote: The Reform UK budget amendment impacts on this initial assessment, reducing the council tax increase from 4.99% to 2%, this reduces the additional funding available by £4.584m and a further decrease of £0.275m in 2027/28 and £0.292m in 2028/29, increasing each year thereafter, representing a cumulative decrease over the 3 years of £14.6m.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy Capital Budget 202627 - 202930.
findings.headline: Ongoing building condition surveys may reveal additional unfunded capital requirements
findings.detail: The council is conducting detailed surveys to assess asset fitness and estate remodelling needs. A £9.9m contingency has been reserved for urgent schemes identified from surveys. This suggests full asset condition is not yet known.
findings.matters: Additional capital requirements beyond the £549.3m programme may emerge from surveys. If contingency proves insufficient, further borrowing or revenue cuts will be required. This indicates asset condition risk is unresolved.

Any urgent in-year schemes will be approved in accordance with our governance arrangements and the key decision limits.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy Capital Budget 202627 - 202930.
findings.headline: Interest rate rises could squeeze capital schemes and revenue budget capacity
findings.detail: The council identifies rising interest rates as a material risk that could add pressure to the revenue budget or force reduction in capital spending. Current projections assume downward rate trajectory, but this remains a medium-term vulnerability.
findings.matters: Interest rate movements directly impact the revenue cost of borrowing and could force the council to cut capital investment or services to maintain debt servicing. This is a material financial exposure.
findings.figures: £6.6m annual borrowing costs
findings.quote: The risk that interest rates rise causing additional pressure to the revenue budget or reducing the amount of capital schemes that can be afforded. This is not expected to happen over the medium-term, all indications are that interest rates are on a downwards trajectory.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy Capital Budget 202627 - 202930.
findings.headline: School buildings at risk of closure without additional £3.7m investment beyond Department for Education funding
findings.detail: The council has identified 16 maintained schools requiring urgent condition works. The Department for Education grant is insufficient. Without additional £3.7m investment, buildings are at risk of closure and future health and safety issues.
findings.matters: School closures impair statutory pupil place provision. Health and safety risks indicate regulatory compliance failures and potential legal liability for the council.
findings.figures: £3.7m investment into 16 maintained educational establishments
findings.quote: This scheme will carry out urgent condition works beyond what is affordable with just the Department for Education grant funding and will see an additional £3.7m investment into 16 maintained educational establishments. Without this investment the buildings are at risk of closure and future health and safety issues.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy Capital Budget 202627 - 202930.
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account faces unfunded £396m liability to meet net zero carbon by 2050
findings.detail: Legislation requires all council houses to achieve net zero carbon by 2050. The HRA business plan identifies a £396m funding gap (at 2025 prices) to meet this requirement. This is not provided within current HRA settlement or capital programme.
findings.matters: This represents a massive unfunded regulatory obligation that will eventually require significant borrowing, revenue investment, or service reduction. It creates long-term financial risk and constraint on the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £396m funding gap (based on 2025 prices)
findings.quote: Legislation has been issued which requires all Council houses to achieve net zero carbon by 2050. findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy Capital Budget 202627 - 202930.
findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales are declining and unreliable, forcing reliance on borrowing
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that asset sales have consistently underperformed on timing and value. The disposals programme is shrinking, meaning future capital receipts will be significantly lower. This unreliability shifts funding risk onto borrowing.
findings.matters: If capital receipts cannot be achieved as forecast, the council must borrow instead, increasing debt burden. This directly affects the sustainability of the capital programme and revenue pressure.
findings.figures: £7.6m estimated receipts over four years; currently planning to finance £9.8m capital schemes from receipts
findings.quote: In the past sales have not been realised at both the level and within the timeframes previously estimated. Council assets available for disposal are also decreasing so the level of capital receipts available in the future will greatly diminish.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy Capital Budget 202627 - 202930.
findings.headline: Borrowing will incur £6.6m annual revenue costs with £225.7m total debt across the period
findings.detail: The council plans to borrow £225.7m to fund capital schemes over four years, with annual debt servicing of £6.6m for interest and repayment charged to revenue budgets from 2026/27 to 2028/29. This creates a structural revenue commitment dependent on interest rates.
findings.matters: Significant debt servicing costs reduce revenue flexibility and increase vulnerability to interest rate movements. A lender needs confidence in the council's capacity to absorb these costs and revenue buffer.
findings.figures: £225.7m total borrowing; £6.6m per annum revenue costs (interest and repayment)

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 202627 - 202930
findings.headline: South Yorkshire Airport City: £57m borrowing approved with funding–spend timing mismatch, forcing council to carry upfront cash-flow risk.
findings.detail: Council approved £57m borrowing in November 2025 for airport reopening. While South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority (SYMCA) grants ultimately cover project costs, the timing of grant funding does not match the planned spend profile, particularly in early years. Large upfront costs must be financed by the council while awaiting grants. Borrowing is expected to commence in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Council is assuming execution risk and cash-flow burden on a major capital project. If spend accelerates or grant payments are delayed, the £57m requirement could increase or need to be refinanced before grant income arrives. Project delays are common in airport/infrastructure work.
findings.figures: £57m total borrowing approved; mix of capital and cash-flow purposes; assumed start 2027/28
findings.quote: On the 27th November 2025 Council approved £57m of borrowing for a mixture of capital and cash-flow purposes to support the reopening of the airport. The report noted that whilst the funding provided from gainshare and other grants via the South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority (SYMCA) covers the costs to be incurred on the project, the profile of funding received doesn't align to the planned spend, especially in the early years with large upfront costs associated with the reopening.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 202627 - 202930
findings.headline: Council maintaining £64m under-borrowed position by using reserves instead of external borrowing, betting entirely on interest rates falling.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is £850m but it has only borrowed £674m externally, leaving £64m unfunded. It is using internal reserves (cash balances) to cover this gap rather than borrowing long-term. The strategy document acknowledges this 'cannot be sustained in the long term' as reserves are being consumed, particularly by the DSG deficit noted above.
findings.matters: When reserves run out (which the DSG deficit will force), the council must borrow £64m+ at whatever market rates exist at that time, with no flexibility. If rates do not fall as forecast, this could lock in significantly higher debt-servicing costs than prudent long-term borrowing would have done today.
findings.figures: CFR 2026/27 £850.459m; external borrowing £674.352m; under-borrowed position £46.672m (declining to £30.3m by 2029/30 as CFR grows faster than borrowing)
findings.quote: The current extent of the under borrowing cannot be sustained in the long term. The reserves and balances are starting to be required as well as the actual amount of reserves available for use being reduced by the increasing dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 202627 - 202930
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit will push council reserves below zero from 2027/28 onwards, creating a structural funding gap.
findings.detail: Reserve balances are forecast to fall from £27.8m in 2025/26 to £4.8m in 2026/27, then turn negative from 2027/28 (−£5.6m) due to accumulated DSG deficit. The council states the funding treatment of this deficit is still awaited from the government settlement due in early February 2026. This negative position persists throughout the forecast period.
findings.matters: Negative reserves signal structural financial imbalance and severely constrain the council's flexibility to manage emergencies, opportunities, or service pressures. A lender would see this as evidence of unsustainable financing and would want to know how the government will resolve it.

findings.paper_title: i12 Cab 140126 General Fund Capital Receipts Programme

findings.detail: The council states that without flexibility to reschedule asset sales, capital programme activities are placed at risk. It has explicitly identified failure to dispose of the planned assets as a risk that will adversely impact capital programme delivery.

findings.headline: Asset disposals carry hidden costs through loss of council revenue streams
findings.detail: The council will incur revenue losses from disposing of income-generating assets. The report explicitly identifies loss of car parking revenues as an example consequence of selling developed land. These revenue impacts require assessment before each disposal but are not quantified.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender must factor that asset sales reduce not just capital balance sheet but also ongoing revenue capacity, potentially worsening the council's revenue budget position

findings.matters: A lender should understand that this council's ability to fund capital programmes via asset sales is not sustainable—there is no long-term plan disclosed for replacing capital receipts as this revenue source dries up
findings.figures: No volume or valuation of remaining disposable assets provided

findings.headline: Capital Programme depends on asset disposals that have a documented history of missing targets
findings.detail: The council's capital programme is substantially funded by capital receipts from property sales. However, previous disposal programmes experienced significant delays—attributed to phasing constraints, local plan development, market conditions, site-specific issues, and environmental strategy work. These delays postponed the capital receipts needed to fund planned projects.
findings.matters: A lender assessing this council's ability to deliver its capital programme needs to know that its primary funding mechanism has a track record of underperformance, creating execution risk on capital spending

findings.paper_title: i8 261125 Audit SoA and AGS 24-25 ISA 260 covering report

findings.detail: The audit identified four adjusted misstatements (one revaluation movement to CIES, three IFRS 16 implementation issues) plus 13 misclassification and disclosure corrections. All were identified and corrected before the accounts were finalized.
findings.matters: Accounting errors requiring auditor identification, even when subsequently corrected, indicate potential weaknesses in the council's financial closedown and accounting treatment processes.

findings.paper_title: i8 261125 Audit SoA and AGS 24-25 ISA 260 covering report
findings.headline: Governance assurance process deemed unusually optimistic, additional validation was required
findings.detail: The council's routine governance review found no new issues, a result the auditors considered unusually optimistic. The council commissioned dip-sampling to validate these findings; Internal Audit endorsed the routine process as reliable. However, the need for this extra validation, combined with auditors identifying additional opportunities to strengthen governance arrangements, suggests the governance assurance framework may not be fully robust.
findings.matters: When auditors feel compelled to seek additional validation of a 'no new issues' finding, it indicates skepticism about the completeness and reliability of routine governance assurance.
findings.figures: None

findings.paper_title: i8 261125 Audit SoA and AGS 24-25 ISA 260 covering report
findings.headline: Five significant governance issues from 2023/24 remain in 2024/25
findings.detail: The council carried forward five significant governance issues from the 2023/24 Annual Governance Statement into 2024/25. No new issues were identified this year, but the five existing issues persist and remain unresolved.
findings.matters: Unresolved governance issues from the prior year that continue into the next year signal control environment weaknesses that have not been remediated.

findings.paper_title: i9 Audit 261125 Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 181125
findings.headline: The budget forecast deteriorated by £6.6m in just Q1 of 2025/26 despite a balanced budget being set in February.
findings.detail: The Council set a balanced budget for 2025/26 in February 2025 using reasonable assumptions, including a 3.99% Council Tax increase (1.99% standard plus 2% Adult Social Care precept) which would generate £5.8m. However, by Q1 2025/26 the Council was already forecasting a £6.6m overspend, driven substantially by Adult Social Care (£6.0m). This rapid deterioration—from balanced to a 4% overspend within one quarter—suggests the underlying cost assumptions in the budget are not reflecting reality and service demand is outpacing projections.
findings.matters: A balanced budget deteriorating to £6.6m overspend in one quarter indicates the Council's budget planning process is not accurately capturing structural cost drivers, particularly in demand-led services.
findings.figures: £6.6m Q1 2025/26 overspend forecast; £6.0m Adult Social Care; balanced budget set February 2025
findings.quote: The Council set a balanced budget for 2025/26 in February 2025 using reasonable assumptions... However, the Council's projected outturn position at quarter 1 2025/26 was a £6.6m overspend again driven substantially by Adults Social care where a £6.0m overspend is forecast.

findings.paper_title: i9 Audit 261125 Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 181125
findings.headline: Governance arrangements for FlyDoncaster Ltd create potential conflicts of interest: CEO and Executive Director of Corporate Resources both hold directorships.
findings.detail: FlyDoncaster Limited's directorships are held by the Council's CEO and Executive Director of Corporate Resources—both among the Council's most senior officers. This creates conflicts of interest because sector guidance expects the CEO to hold an independent oversight and scrutiny role for the entity. The auditor notes that 'conflicts of interest can arise when any individual holds a council role which involves oversight and scrutiny of the entity, while also holding a position with the entity.' Additionally, the Section 151 Officer and Monitoring Officer—who should provide checks—report to the Executive Director of Corporate Resources, raising questions about independence. The auditor flagged this as exposing the Council to 'a risk of both real and perceived conflicts of interest.'
findings.matters: Conflicts of interest in governance around a £145m investment undermine oversight effectiveness. Lenders and regulators expect clear separation of roles to ensure project scrutiny is genuinely independent.
findings.figures: Two most senior officers holding directorships; £145.4m project under governance
findings.quote: At the time of review, FDL's directorships remained filled by the Council's CEO and Executive Director of Corporate Resources, both of whom are among the Council's most senior officers. This raises questions around the management of potential conflicts of interest... Sector guidance envisages a key role for Council CEOs (alongside the two other statutory officers – the Section 151 Officer and Monitoring Officer) in overseeing and scrutinising company performance from a council perspective.

findings.paper_title: i9 Audit 261125 Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 181125
findings.headline: The South Yorkshire Airport City project carries £145.4m in planned investment with significant unresolved financial and commercial risks.
findings.detail: Doncaster is investing £145.4m to reopen Doncaster Sheffield Airport via FlyDoncaster Ltd, a Special Purpose Vehicle. The project involves £105.2m in subsidised interest loans, with the subsidy estimated between £53.5m and £134.5m using a 5.3% discount rate over ten years. The Outline Business Case projected positive EBITDA by year 4; the Final Business Case now projects year 8, with losses not recouped until year 15. SYMCA postponed its decision in February 2025 pending further assurance work before releasing £5.3m from its annual gainshare. On 9 September 2025, SYMCA voted to release up to £160m funding. However, the auditor found 'a high level of risk and uncertainty in relation to the project's viability' and noted there is currently 'no clear, final delivery plan against which to assess the ultimate risk to the Council.'
findings.matters: This project represents 1.5 times the Council's current reserves and carries both commercial (passenger forecast) and delivery risk. Lenders would be concerned about the Council's ability to absorb cost overruns or exit the project if circumstances deteriorate.
findings.figures: £145.4m funding requirement; £105.2m subsidised loans; subsidy £53.5m-£134.5m; breakeven year 8; payback year 15; SYMCA approved up to £160m total funding
findings.quote: The Council's February 2025 Cabinet report identified a £145.4m funding requirement to reopen Doncaster Sheffield Airport... A major element is £105.2m in subsidised interest loans to FDL, with the subsidy—based on the gap from commercial rates—estimated between £53.5m and £134.5m... the variations in financial performance between the OBC and FBC indicate a high level of risk and uncertainty in relation to the project's viability at this stage.

findings.paper_title: i9 Audit 261125 Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 181125
findings.headline: General Fund reserves have fallen to £94.5m with only £12.7m unallocated—just 7 days of operational cover.
findings.detail: The Council closed 2024/25 with £94.475m total reserves (down from £103.480m), of which only £12.662m is unallocated. This represents just 7 days of operational cover. The auditor notes this is 'modest for a Council of this scale, type and complexity' and observes that 'reserves remained stable, though are not excessive.' Worryingly, the Council set its 2025/26 budget without planning to increase reserves despite having a relatively favourable settlement. The limited buffer is particularly concerning given emerging pressures: the DSG deficit materialising in 2028, Adult Social Care overspends, and the airport project risks.
findings.matters: A seven-day cash buffer leaves the Council highly vulnerable. Any sustained demand pressure (particularly in Adult Social Care) or a cash timing issue could force emergency borrowing or service cuts.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £94.475m; unallocated reserves £12.662m; represents 7 days operational cover; down from £103.480m prior year
findings.quote: the Council closed the year with a General Fund balance of £94.475m, comprising £12.662m in unallocated reserves and £81.814m in earmarked reserves—down from £103.480m the previous year... the level of uncommitted reserves is modest for a Council of this scale, equating to just seven days of operational cover.

findings.paper_title: i9 Audit 261125 Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 181125
findings.headline: Adult Social Care is running £6-7.5m over budget annually with no clear plan to bring costs under control.
findings.detail: The Council overspent by £7.6m on Adult Social Care in 2024/25, attributed to higher numbers of older people in care homes, higher average costs, and higher activity in Supported Living. By Q1 2025/26, this service was already forecasting a £6.0m overspend. The auditor notes explicitly that 'it is not clear at this stage that the Council has a fully costed plan to manage demand to a point where it can control costs in this area within allocated budgets.' External factors are worsening the position: residents losing NHS-funded Continuing Healthcare eligibility and inherited costs from young people with SEND transitioning to adulthood.
findings.matters: Demand-led service overspends of this magnitude and persistence indicate structural problems in budget planning or service delivery. Continued overspends erode reserves and weaken financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £7.6m overspend 2024/25; £6.0m forecast overspend Q1 2025/26; no fully costed mitigation plan identified
findings.quote: The Council reported a £7.6m overspend on Adult Social Care budgets in 2024/25... However, it is not clear at this stage that the Council has a fully costed plan to manage demand to a point where it can control costs in this area within allocated budgets.

findings.paper_title: i9 Audit 261125 Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 181125
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £37.6m and is forecast to hit £45.1m in 2025/26, consuming 50% of the council's reserves.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit continues to accelerate despite Council mitigation efforts. The High Needs Block overspent by £12.3m in 2024/25 (of which £8.0m was planned). Additional pressures came from special school funding, EHCP support in mainstream schools, and SEN funding totalling £4.3m. The deficit forecast for 2025/26 has risen to £45.1m from £42.4m forecast just one year earlier. The cumulative deficit now represents around 50% of the Council's combined unallocated and earmarked general fund reserves. Critically, the statutory override protecting the Council ends March 2028, after which the Council becomes liable for the full deficit.
findings.matters: A DSG liability of this scale materialising in 2028 would force the Council to either fund it from reserves (depleting them entirely) or cut services. Lenders would treat this as a real contingent liability affecting borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £37.6m deficit at 31 March 2025; £45.1m forecast for 2025/26 (up from £42.4m one year earlier); represents 50% of combined reserves; statutory override ends March 2028
findings.quote: Doncaster Council ended 2024/25 with a £12.3m overspend on the High Needs Block, contributing to a total DSG deficit of £37.6m... The forecast DSG deficit for 2025/26 rose to £45.1m as of June 2025, up from £42.4m forecasted in June 2024. The cumulative deficit is now around 50% of the Council's combined unallocated and earmarked general fund reserves, posing a significant financial risk.

findings.paper_title: i8 Audit 261125 Appendix A City of Doncaster Council - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: £457m of property assets not revalued in year; £1.4m valuation variance recorded as auditor-disagreed misstatement

Auditors disagreed and recorded this as an unadjusted misstatement, meaning it remains uncorrected but known. This creates a recorded valuation gap on a significant asset class.
findings.matters: A known £1.4m valuation variance on £457m of properties represents acknowledged imprecision in the asset base; auditor-recorded misstatements indicate management and auditor disagreement on materiality thresholds, which is a governance concern
findings.figures: £457m of assets not revalued; £1.4m variance; increases value at year end

However, given this movement is in excess of triviality, this has been recorded as an unadjusted misstatement

findings.paper_title: i8 Audit 261125 Appendix A City of Doncaster Council - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: £3.5m property revaluation movements incorrectly charged to revenue instead of reserves
findings.detail: Audit sample testing identified a £3.0m revaluation movement incorrectly recorded in the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement (CIES) rather than the Revaluation Reserve. Subsequent review of all revaluations charged to revenue identified seven additional assets totalling £0.5m with the same error. Total: £3.5m. This arises from property holdings totalling £1.63bn for land and buildings and council dwellings. Management has agreed to correct.
findings.matters: Errors in revaluation accounting mask the true movement in asset values and distort reported revenue expenditure; the pervasiveness of this error (multiple assets) indicates control weaknesses over how major property movements are classified between capital and revenue
findings.figures: £3.5m total misstatement (£3.0m + £0.5m); property holdings £1.63bn

In total, £3.5 million had been inappropriately recognised as expenditure in the CIES

findings.paper_title: i8 Audit 261125 Appendix A City of Doncaster Council - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: Three significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements; auditors not satisfied council has proper resources management
findings.detail: Grant Thornton identified three significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in use of resources. The auditors state they are not satisfied the council has made proper arrangements. Full findings set out in the separate Auditor's Annual Report presented to 26 November 2025 Audit Committee.
findings.matters: VFM significant weaknesses are governance red flags indicating the council lacks proper controls over resource management and value for money; this represents a reputational risk and can trigger enhanced regulatory scrutiny affecting credit ratings and lending decisions

findings.paper_title: i8 Audit 261125 Appendix A City of Doncaster Council - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting errors totalling £33m in first-year implementation, including £24.5m airport liability understatement
findings.detail: The council's first-year implementation of the new IFRS 16 leases standard revealed material errors: Doncaster Sheffield Airport's rental increases from 2029 onwards were omitted from liability calculations, understating both right-of-use assets and lease liabilities by £24.5m. Schools PFI contingent rents were incorrectly processed requiring £7.8m adjustment. Five additional leases were miscategorised for £0.8m error. Management has agreed to correct all adjustments. Total IFRS 16 right-of-use assets recognised: £185.6m.
findings.matters: These errors represent a significant control failure in implementing a major new accounting standard affecting over £185m of balance sheet assets; the number and scale of errors suggest underlying control weaknesses in asset classification and lease liability calculation that could persist
